ECO2021 Basic Macroeconomics
                                       Final Exam

Section A: Multiple Choice (20 Questions  2 points each, 40 points total)
Answer ALL questions on the multiple choice answer sheet. Choose only one answer, the best answer.


1.       In the poorer countries in Africa, people consume a substantial amount of food that they produce
        for themselves. Because of this,
B
      A. reported inflation is biased upwards, as peoples’ cost of living is actually lower than reported.
       B.  reported real GDP is biased downwards, as the value of the food produced for themselves is
            not included when calculating GDP.
       C.  reported real GDP per capita is biased upwards, as the people have a higher living standard.
      D.  inflation is biased downwards, as home food production keeps prices low.
       E.  None of the above answers are correct.


2.      Assume we know that over the last 5 years, the velocity of M2 has been decreasing by 1% per
        year. Meanwhile, inflation has been constant at 2% per year, and real GDP has increased by 4%
        per year. According to the Quantity Theory of Money, we can conclude that:
D
      A. Money supply has grown by about 1% per year.
       B. Money supply has grown by about 3% per year.
       C. Money supply has grown by about 5% per year.
      D. Money supply has grown by about 7% per year.
       E. None of the above answers are correct.


3.      Over the last few decades, unemployment rates in many European countries have been on
       average significantly higher than those in the United States. This is partially due to the fact that:
D
      A. The U.S. has laws that made it difficult to fire workers for discriminatory reasons.
       B. The European countries have a much lower share of young people in the labor force.
       C. The US has a lower savings rate.
      D. The European countries have more generous unemployment benefits.
       E. None of the above answers are correct.


4.      Suppose a mobile phone manufacturer pays $60 million for the battery, screen, chips, and other
        parts to make a phone, $30 million to rent the factory, and $20 million for labor to assemble the
        parts into a phone. The manufacturer sells the phones it made for $120 million, and takes home
         profits of $10 million. How much is the manufacturer’s value-added?
C
      A. $10
       B. $30
       C. $60
      D. $110
       E. None of the above answers are correct.

5.      Suppose that last year, Private Savings (SP) = 90 billion, Government Spending (G) = 200 billion,
       Investment (I) = 70 billion, and that trade was balanced (NX=0). What was Taxation (T) equal to?
E
      A. 160 billion
       B. 200 billion
       C. 220 billion
      D. 270 billion
       E. None of the above answers are correct.


6.       Last year CPI = 100, and Real GDP = 1000. This year CPI = 103, and Real GDP = 1010.
       Nominal GDP growth was roughly equal to:
D
      A. 1%
       B. 2%
       C. 3%
      D. 4%
       E. 5%


7.      The four "Asian Economic Tigers" (Hong Kong, Singapore, South Korea, and Taiwan) achieved
       high economic growth in the 1970s and 1980s in part because of the following factors EXCEPT :
C
      A. Their labor force participation rates increased as women entered the labor force.
       B. They had very high savings rates, and high investment.
       C.  Their governments protected the important industries from external competition.
      D. They successfully controlled their population growth.
       E.  Their governments devoted many resources to education.


8.      Suppose the economy is experiencing high inflation, of about 20% per year. Carrying out tight
       monetary policy to cause disinflation will result in:
C
      A.  the short run cost of higher inflation, but the long run benefit of higher economic growth
       B.  the short run benefit of lower inflation, but the long run cost of higher unemployment
       C.  the short run cost of higher unemployment, but the long run benefit of lower inflation
      D.  the short run benefit of higher economic growth, but the long run cost of higher unemployment
       E. None of the above answers are correct


9.       All of the following are reasonable arguments against central banks adopting a zero inflation rate
         target, EXCEPT:
A
      A. A zero inflation rate will cause the price level to become unstable in the long-run.
       B. A zero inflation target makes deflation (and its undesirable effects) more likely.
       C. A zero inflation rate prevents the central bank from achieving a negative real interest rate,
          which may be desirable during deep recessions.
      D. A zero inflation target based on the CPI would actually result in some deflation, because of
         CPI measurement problems.
       E. A zero inflation rate makes it more difficult for the labor market to adjust to equilibrium.



                                                                                              1

10.     Suppose that the government previously had a balanced budget. If the government increases
       government spending and starts to run a budget deficit, according to the AD-AS model which of
        the following will NOT occur in the short run:
E
      A. Real interest rates will rise.
       B. Consumption will be increase.
       C. Government debt will increase.
      D. Aggregate Demand will increase.
       E. Unemployment will rise.


11.     Suppose that a Central Bank has a simple monetary policy reaction function, where it sets the
         target real interest rate (r*) equal to double the inflation rate:
                 r* = 2 
       Suppose that the inflation rate increases from 1% to 2%, this will mean that the central bank will
       change its nominal interest rate target …
D
      A. from 2% to 3%.
       B. from 2% to 4%.
       C. from 3% to 5%.
      D. from 3% to 6%.
       E.  from 3% to 7%.


12. During the Great Depression in the 1930s, many countries – experiencing very high unemployment –
    decided to abandon the Gold Standard (which linked paper money to a fixed amount of gold) and rely
    on fiat currency. They did this to allow the country’s Central Bank to drastically increase the money
     supply. Given your understanding of the Keynesian model, what likely happened after a country
    abandoned the Gold Standard?
B
      A. The country suffered from a severe loss of investor confidence, worsening the recession.
       B. The more expansionary monetary policy allowed the economy to recover more quickly.
       C.  Businesses stopped using money and started relying on barter, allowing production to increase.
      D. People abandoned holding the currency and prices soared, resulting in hyper-inflation and the
           shops becoming empty of merchandize.
       E. The international foreign exchange markets stopped trading the country’s currency, effectively
            cutting the country off from international trade


13.     Which of the following will contribute to long-term economic growth, increasing productive
        capacity in the long run?
B
      A. Growth in consumption expenditures.
       B. Improvements in the education system.
       C.  Increased risk aversion in the banking system.
      D. Increasing the growth rate of money supply.
       E.  Decreasing taxation.





                                                                                              2

14.     Suppose the inflation rate is −1% (we have deflation). Because of the zero-lower-bound on
       nominal interest rates:
D
      A. The real interest rate is undefined in this situation.
       B. The lowest real interest rate possible is about −1%.
       C. The lowest real interest rate possible is about 0%.
      D. The lowest real interest rate possible is about 1%.
       E.  There is no restriction on the real interest rate.



15.     Assume that Y = C + I + G , and that NX = 0. Suppose that I = 3000 ; G = 3000 ; T = 2000
      And that the consumption function is: C = 7500 + 0.75 (Y – T )
        In the simple Keynesian cross model, what is the short-run equilibrium level of output (Y)?
D
      A. 12,000
       B. 17,500
       C. 40,000
      D. 48,000
       E. None of the above answers are correct

17. Suppose there is a negative supply shock and the AS curve shifts to the left. This causes the
     equilibrium to move along the AD curve. Which of the following will NOT occur in the short run?
B
      A. There is a decrease in the aggregate quantity demanded of goods and services.
       B. The nominal interest rate falls.
       C. The unemployment rate rises.
      D. Real GDP falls.
       E. The inflation rate rises.

18.     Suppose that the US Federal Reserve were to significantly raise their target for the Fed Funds rate
      (US inter-bank interest rate). What will this do to the exchange rate of the US dollar and the US
        trade deficit?
 A
      A. The US dollar will appreciate, and the US trade deficit will get larger.
       B. The US dollar will appreciate, and the US trade deficit will get smaller.
       C. The US dollar will depreciate, and the US trade deficit will get larger.
      D. The US dollar will depreciate, and the US trade deficit will get smaller.
       E.  This change will not affect either the US dollar exchange rate or the US trade deficit.



19.     The benefits of capital inflows into a country include all of the following EXCEPT:
D
      A.  It enlarges the pool of loanable funds available.
       B.  It allows a larger amount of investment by the economy.
       C.  It can result in higher long run economic growth rates.
      D.  It increases the domestic household savings rate.
       E.  It allows the government to borrow at a lower interest rate.


20.     According to economists, a fixed exchange rate can be beneficial, especially for smaller
       economies, because:
C
      A. Fixed exchange rates can gain revenue for the government, as the government can sell its own
           currency to raise revenue.
       B. Exchange rates under a fixed exchange rate regime can be more easily changed than exchange
             rates under a floating exchange rate regime.
       C. A fixed exchange rate reduces international uncertainty and risk, and promotes international
            trade and international investments.
      D.  International capital movements are not necessarily good for the economy; capital movements
           can be more easily monitored and controlled under a fixed exchange rate regime.
       E. None of the above answers are correct.

Section B: Short Questions (4 Questions, 60 points total)

Answer ALL of the following questions. Justify your answer, but keep your answers as short and as clear
as possible.

1. The Quantity Equation of Money describes the Long Run link between money, velocity, prices, and real
GDP (or alternatively, the relationship between the growth rates of money, the growth rate of velocity,
inflation, and real GDP growth). Suppose you are put in charge of the central bank in an economy where
both inflation and real interest rates have been about 2% over the past decade. You have just been
informed that your predecessor had increased the money supply by about 5% a year over the past decade.

a) Assume that both velocity and the real GDP growth rate are stable. From the information given above,
what can you deduce about the growth rate of real GDP in this economy?                      (2 points)

Since:  growth rate of money = inflation + GDP growth
  GDP growth = 5% – 2% = 3%

b) Suppose you decide that 2% inflation is too low a rate, and that you need to take steps to increase
inflation to 5% a year in the long run. Assuming that velocity remains as in part (a) above, to achieve your
goal, what is the new growth rate of money supply that you should target for this economy?     (2 points)

Since:  growth rate of money = inflation + GDP growth
  growth rate of money = 5% + 3% = 8%


c) Look forward to ten years later, to when you will be retiring as central bank governor. Assume that your
policy has successfully maintained a 5% annual inflation rate, and that not much else has changed about
the economy. What do you expect nominal interest rates and real interest rates to be, 10 year later at
your retirement, compared to the time when your predecessor had retired ten years before?      (2 points)

Real interest rates should be unaffected, because of the long run neutrality of money.
Real interest rates were 2% so, ten years later they should still be 2%
Nominal interest rates = Real interest rates + Inflation = 5% + 2% = 7%

[access or contact details]
growth has increased by 1%. That is, the annual real GDP growth rate is permanently higher by 1%
compared to before. How would you change your target for the growth rate of money supply, assuming
that you still want to target a 5% annual inflation rate?                                        (2 points)

Since:  growth rate of money = inflation + GDP growth
  growth rate of money = 5% + 4% = 9%

2. Political instability (because of the Vietnam War and other issues) was a major worry in the US in the
1960s. The Federal Reserve at that time tried to support the US government by loosening monetary policy
– keeping interest rates low in order to hold down unemployment rates. Inflation, from about 1% in the
early 1960s, had increased to more than 5% by the early 1970s.

Assume that the economy starts in long run equilibrium.

i) Describe the short run effects of loosening monetary policy. What happens to inflation, GDP,
unemployment, interest rates (both nominal and real), investment and consumption?

Draw an AD-AS diagram to illustrate your arguments.                                        (7 points)


In the short run, if the Federal Reserve loosens monetary policy (sets interest rates lower
regardless of inflation), this will increase Investment, which will increase Aggregate Demand. It
will shift the AD curve to the right in the AS-AD model. At the new short run equilibrium, inflation
will be higher, output (GDP) will be higher, and unemployment will be lower.

The Federal Reserve is targeting lower real interest rates, so real interest rates will be lower.
However, it is ambiguous what will happen to nominal interest rates at the short run equilibrium.
 Nominal interest rates (i) = real interest rate (r) + inflation ()
Real interest rates are lower, but inflation is higher, so nominal interest rates may be a bit higher
or a bit lower than before.

Since the Federal Reserve has set real interest rates lower, investment will be higher.
Since output is higher, consumption will be higher.

ii) Describe the long run effects of loosening monetary policy. What happens in the long run, to inflation,
GDP, unemployment, interest rates (both nominal and real), investment and consumption?
Draw another AD-AS diagram to illustrate your arguments.                                    (7 points)


Since at the short run equilibrium, inflation exceeds inflation expectations; in the long run,
inflation expectations will increase. Increase in inflation expectations causes the Aggregate
Supply curve to shift upwards (or to the left), and inflation will rise and output will fall. In the long
run equilibrium, the AS curve shifts up enough so that output (GDP) is back down to the original
level (before the Federal Reserve loosened policy). At this new equilibrium, inflation will be higher
again, output will be at the original level Y*, and unemployment will also rise back again to the
original level.

With the much higher inflation, the Federal Reserve will be forced to raise its real interest rate
target. At the long run equilibrium, real interest rates will be back to the original level, the level
before the Federal Reserve loosened policy.

Since both real interest rates and inflation are higher compared to the short run equilibrium,
nominal interest rates will be higher than at the short run equilibrium. They will also higher than
they were originally (before the Federal Reserve loosened policy).

Since the real interest rates have increased back to the original level, investment will be lower
than at the short run equilibrium. Investment will fall back to the original level before the Federal
Reserve loosened policy.

Since output has fallen back to the original level, consumption will also fall back to the original
level before the Federal Reserve loosened policy.

3. Suppose there is a small fictional country in the Mediterranean, called San Marco, that wishes to keep its
currency, the Marco dollar (M$), pegged versus the Euro (€), at an exchange rate of M$100 = €4. If the
exchange rate were freely determined in the foreign exchange markets, the exchange rate would stabilize at
M$100 = €5.

a) Illustrate this situation in the market for foreign exchange (showing the supply and demand of local
currency, and the fixed exchange rate). Is the Marco dollar overvalued or undervalued? How does this
affect Net Exports?                                                                           (6 points)

The Marco dollar is currently undervalued. At the official rate, there is more demand than supply
for the Marco dollar. Since the exchange rate is depreciated below the market rate, there will be
more exports and less imports. Therefore, Net Exports will be higher than at the market rate.

b) Suppose the San Marco central bank can freely buy or sell foreign currency for local currency. What
does the San Marco central bank need to do, in terms of buying or selling foreign currency for local
currency, in order to maintain the pegged exchange rate? Illustrate in the diagram that you have drawn for
part a), the amount of local currency that the central bank must buy or sell. What will happen to the foreign
currency reserves of the San Marco central bank?                                              (4 points)

To keep the exchange rate at the official rate, the central bank of San Marco must sell local
currency equal to the excess demand for local currency in the market. When the sell local
currency, they are also buying foreign currency. The foreign currency reserves of the San Marco
central bank will rise over time.

c) What will happen to the money supply because of the actions of the San Marco central bank in
maintaining the exchange rate peg? Will this have an expansionary or contractionary effect on the
economy?                                                                                    (4 points)

Since the central bank of San Marco is selling local currency in the foreign exchange market, the
amount of money in the economy will increase. Money supply increases over time. This will have
an expansionary effect on the economy, and inflation will rise.

4. The following statements are correct descriptions of the macroeconomy. Explain the economic
reasoning behind the following statements in your own words. Use the standard versions of the economic
models in the lecture notes and the textbook. You must explain why the statement is true. In the exam, if
you only write down a mathematical formula without any economic explanation, you will not receive
credit.                                                  (3 points each)

               a.  In the Keynesian consumption function, when the autonomous consumption expenditure
               changes by certain amount, total consumption and the short run equilibrium level of
                output changes by a larger amount than the increase in autonomous consumption.

              b.  The tax multiplier is smaller in size than the government spending multiplier. That is, if
              government spending increases or net tax decreases by the same amount, the change in
                equilibrium output induced by the change in government spending is larger than a similar
                  size change in taxation.

               c.  Recessions in a large open economy like the US can lead to recessions in other countries
                  that trade with the US, especially if they are a small open economy.

              d.   If the central bank increases money supply, then, consumption, investment, and net
                exports increase, thus increasing the short-run equilibrium level of output. Why do each
                of these components of Aggregate Demand increase?

               e. A lender of last resort can reduce the possibility of bank runs and panics, and so, will
               reduce the occurrence of deep recessions and economic depressions.

                  f.  An open market purchase of government securities by the central bank will usually
                decrease the nominal interbank interest rate, unless the nominal interbank interest rate is
                equal to zero.

              g.   If all goods and services are traded internationally and there are no trade costs, then the
                 real exchange rate should always be equal to 1.

              h.  In reality, the actual money multiplier – the ratio of the increase in broad money supply
             (M2) that results from an increase in base money (M0) – is less than that amount implied
              by the reserve requirement, i.e. the multiplier is less than 1/RR, where RR is the required
                 reserve ratio.

Answers
               a.  In the Keynesian consumption function, when the autonomous consumption expenditure
               changes by certain amount, total consumption and the short run equilibrium level of
                output changes by a larger amount than the increase in autonomous consumption.
The increase in autonomous expenditure raises output, which leads to higher income. Higher income
further increases consumption demand, which further increases output. Such positive feedback leads to
consumption and the short run equilibrium level of output increasing more than the original shock (the
spending multiplier is larger than 1).

              b.  The tax multiplier is smaller in size than the government spending multiplier. That is, if
              government spending increases or net tax decreases by the same amount, the change in



                                                                                              9

equilibrium output induced by the change in government spending is larger than a similar
                  size change in taxation.
The change in net tax directly affects disposable income, of which only a fraction (mpc) contributes to the
PAE. The change in government spending fully contributes to the PAE. Therefore, the tax multiplier is
smaller than the government spending multiplier.

               c.  Recessions in a large open economy like the US can lead to recessions in other countries
                  that trade with the US, especially if they are a small open economy.
When the large country goes into recession, its demand for foreign output decreases. This reduces the NX
component of the PAE in countries that export to the large country. This has a big impact, because large
countries buy a lot, and will form a significant part of a small country’s exports.

              d.   If the central bank increases money supply, then, consumption, investment, and net
                exports increase, thus increasing the short-run equilibrium level of output. Why do each
                of these components of Aggregate Demand increase?
An increase in money supply decreases the nominal interest rate. Because prices are sticky in the short
run, the real interest rate also decreases. Planed consumption and investment are decreasing functions of
the real interest rate, so both consumption and investment will increase. The exchange rate will depreciate
when interest rates fall, so net exports will also increase. Consumption will increase further because of the
multiplier effect. This causes Aggregate Demand, and short run equilibrium output, to rise.

               e. A lender of last resort can reduce the possibility of bank runs and panics, and so, will
               reduce the occurrence of deep recessions and economic depressions.
A lender of last resort guarantees that banks have enough cash reserves to pay back the deposits of their
depositors. Knowing this, the depositors have less incentive to withdraw their deposits from the bank if
they suspect that a bank run may occur. This reduces the possibility of bank runs occurring.

                  f.  An open market purchase of government securities by the central bank will usually
                decrease the nominal interbank interest rate, unless the nominal interbank interest rate is
                equal to zero.
In an open market purchase, commercial banks receive reserves from the central bank. The supply of
reserves increases lending in the interbank market, so the nominal interest rate decreases. However, when
nominal interbank interest rate is equal to zero, commercial banks will just hold on to the reserves, as
lending them out will not yield any interest income.

              g.   If all goods and services are traded internationally and there are no trade costs, then the
                 real exchange rate should always be equal to 1.
      The real exchange rate measures the relative real costs of goods and services in the consumption
        basket. If it is not equal to 1, then consumers can sell the goods and services in the more expensive
        countries and purchase the goods and services in the cheaper ones. This will move prices so that
        the real exchange rate becomes 1.

              h.  In reality, the actual money multiplier – the ratio of the increase in broad money supply
             (M2) that results from an increase in base money (M0) – is less than that amount implied
              by the reserve requirement, i.e. the multiplier is less than 1/RR, where RR is the required
                 reserve ratio.
Since banks will hold some excess reserves, and the non-banking sector will hold some cash, not all of the
newly created money will go through the money multiplier process. Deposits will not increase by the full



                                                                                             10

amount possible as not all of the base money created becomes bank required reserves. Hence deposits will
increase by less than the ratio 1/RR
